hook: A day on Venus is longer than its *year.*
hookVo: A day on Venus is longer than its year.

scenes.vo: Venus takes about two hundred and forty-three Earth days to spin around just once.

scenes.sub: Its year ends before its day does.
scenes.vo: But it circles the Sun in only two hundred and twenty-five. So its year ends... before its day does.

caption:
A day on Venus is longer than its year. 🪐

One spin takes ~243 Earth days, but one orbit around the Sun takes only ~225.

hook: The Sun holds *99.8%* of the Solar System's mass.
hookVo: The Sun holds about ninety-nine point eight percent of all the mass in our Solar System.

scenes.vo: Every planet, moon and asteroid combined makes up just zero point two percent.
And most of that leftover belongs to Jupiter. Earth is barely a speck.

caption:
The Sun holds about 99.8% of all the mass in our Solar System. ☀️

Every planet, moon and asteroid together is just ~0.2%, and most of that is Jupiter.

hook: A sugar cube of neutron star weighs about a *billion tons.*
hookVo: A sugar cube of neutron star material would weigh about a billion tons.

scenes.vo: A neutron star squeezes more mass than our Sun into a ball only about twenty kilometres wide.
And the fastest one spins seven hundred and sixteen times every second.

caption:
A sugar-cube-sized piece of a neutron star would weigh about a billion tons. 🌟

They pack more than the Sun's mass into a ball ~20 km wide, and the fastest spins 716 times a second.

hook: Footprints on the Moon could last *millions of years.*
hookVo: The footprints left on the Moon could last for millions of years.

scenes.vo: The Moon has no wind and no rain, so nothing wipes the dust away.
So the prints left in nineteen sixty-nine are almost certainly still there today.

caption:
Astronaut footprints on the Moon could last for millions of years. 👣🌕

With no wind or rain, nothing wipes them away.

hook: About *1.3 million* Earths could fit inside the Sun.
hookVo: About one point three million Earths could fit inside the Sun.

scenes.vo: The Sun is so big that about one point three million Earths could fit inside it.

scenes.ital: Some stars would swallow it whole.
scenes.vo: And yet, it's only an average star. Some giants out there could swallow it whole.

caption:
About 1.3 million Earths could fit inside the Sun. ☀️🌍

And it's only an average-sized star.

hook: Saturn would *float* in water.
hookSub: If you had a big enough bathtub.
hookVo: Saturn would float in water.

scenes.vo: Saturn is mostly hydrogen and helium, so on average it's less dense than water.

scenes.big: You'd just need a bathtub *bigger than Saturn.*
scenes.vo: So in theory it would float. You'd just need a bathtub big enough.

caption:
Saturn would float in water. 🪐🛁

Its average density (~0.69 g/cm³) is lower than water's.

hook: The sunlight you see is about *8 minutes* old.
hookVo: The sunlight you see right now is about eight minutes old.

scenes.sub: Light is fast, but space is huge.
scenes.vo: Light from the Sun takes about eight minutes and twenty seconds to reach us.

scenes.big: If the Sun vanished, you wouldn't *know* for 8 minutes.
scenes.ital: It would still look like it's shining.
scenes.vo: So if the Sun suddenly disappeared, we wouldn't notice for eight whole minutes.

caption: The sunlight hitting you right now left the Sun about 8 minutes ago. ☀️⏱️

hook: There are more stars than grains of *sand* on Earth's beaches.
hookVo: There are more stars in the universe than grains of sand on every beach on Earth.

scenes.vo: The observable universe holds billions of galaxies, each with billions of stars.
Scientists estimate that's more than every grain of sand on every beach combined.

caption: There are more stars in the universe than grains of sand on all of Earth's beaches. ✨🏖️

hook: A year on Mercury lasts just *88 days.*
hookVo: A year on Mercury lasts just eighty-eight days.

scenes.vo: Mercury races around the Sun in only eighty-eight Earth days.
But from one sunrise to the next takes a hundred and seventy-six Earth days. Two whole Mercury years.

caption: A year on Mercury is only 88 Earth days, but one sunrise-to-sunrise day lasts 176. ☿️

hook: Mars has a volcano *2.5 times* taller than Everest.
hookVo: Mars has a volcano about two and a half times taller than Mount Everest.

scenes.vo: Olympus Mons rises about twenty-two kilometres high.

scenes.sub: The biggest volcano in the Solar System.
scenes.vo: And its base is around six hundred kilometres wide. The biggest volcano in the Solar System.

caption: Olympus Mons on Mars is ~22 km tall, about 2.5x Mount Everest. 🌋🔴

hook: Space is completely *silent.*
hookVo: Space is completely silent.

scenes.ital: Space is almost a perfect vacuum.
scenes.vo: Sound travels by making air vibrate, but space is almost completely empty.

scenes.big: Explosions in space make *no sound* at all.
scenes.vo: So even a massive explosion out there would make no sound at all. Sorry, movies.

caption:
Space is completely silent. 🤫🌌

Sound needs air (or something) to travel through, and space is nearly a perfect vacuum.

hook: Jupiter has a storm *bigger than Earth.*
hookSub: And it's been raging for centuries.
hookVo: Jupiter has a storm that's bigger than the entire Earth.

scenes.vo: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a giant storm, wider than the whole Earth.
Its winds blow faster than four hundred kilometres an hour, and it's been raging for well over a hundred and fifty years.

caption: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm wider than the entire Earth. 🌪️🪐

hook: When dinosaurs lived, days were *shorter.*
hookVo: When dinosaurs were alive, a day on Earth was shorter.

scenes.vo: Seventy million years ago, a day lasted only about twenty-three and a half hours.

scenes.ital: Days keep getting a tiny bit longer.
scenes.vo: The Moon's pull works like a brake, so our days keep getting slightly longer.

caption:
70 million years ago, a day on Earth lasted only ~23.5 hours. 🦖🌍

The Moon's tidal pull is slowly slowing our planet's spin.

hook: An octopus has three *hearts.*
hookVo: An octopus has three hearts.

scenes.sub: Two for the gills, one for the body.
scenes.vo: Two hearts pump blood to the gills, and the third pumps it around the rest of the body.
And its blood is blue, because it uses copper instead of iron to carry oxygen.

caption: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood. 🐙💙

hook: A blue whale's heart can weigh about *180 kg.*
hookVo: A blue whale's heart can weigh about a hundred and eighty kilograms.

scenes.vo: That's heavier than two grown adults put together.
The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived. Bigger than any dinosaur.

caption:
A blue whale's heart can weigh around 180 kg. 🐋❤️

It's the largest animal known to have ever lived.

hook: One jellyfish can, in a way, live *forever.*
hookVo: There's a jellyfish that can, in a way, live forever.

scenes.vo: When it's hurt or stressed, this tiny jellyfish can turn back into its baby stage...
...and start its whole life over again. Scientists call it biologically immortal.

caption: The 'immortal jellyfish' (Turritopsis dohrnii) can turn back into its baby stage and start life over. 🪼♾️

hook: Over *80%* of the ocean is still unexplored.
hookVo: More than eighty percent of the ocean has never been explored.

scenes.vo: Most of the deep ocean has never been seen by humans.
In fact, we have more detailed maps of Mars than of our own seafloor.

caption:
More than 80% of the ocean remains unexplored. 🌊

We have better maps of Mars than of our own seafloor.

hook: Sharks don't have a single *bone.*
hookVo: Sharks don't have a single bone in their bodies.

scenes.ital: The same stuff in your nose and ears.
scenes.vo: Their skeleton is made of cartilage, the same flexible stuff in your nose and ears.
It's lighter and bendier than bone, which helps them turn fast and save energy.

caption:
Sharks don't have a single bone. 🦈

Their skeleton is made entirely of cartilage.

hook: Some sharks can live for about *400 years.*
hookVo: Some sharks can live for around four hundred years.

scenes.vo: Scientists estimate the Greenland shark can live for around four hundred years.

scenes.sub: Some alive today may be older than the USA.
scenes.vo: It grows only about a centimetre a year, so some swimming today may be older than the United States.

caption: Greenland sharks can live for around 400 years. 🦈⏳

hook: Octopuses can *taste* with their arms.
hookVo: Octopuses can taste with their arms.

scenes.vo: Their suckers are packed with chemical sensors, so they taste whatever they touch.

scenes.sub: Each arm almost thinks for itself.
scenes.vo: And about two thirds of its neurons are in its arms, so each arm can almost think for itself.

caption: Octopuses taste with their suckers, and about two-thirds of their neurons are in their arms. 🐙🧠

hook: You can see the Great Barrier Reef from *space.*
hookVo: You can see the Great Barrier Reef from space.

scenes.vo: It stretches for about two thousand three hundred kilometres.
It's the largest structure on Earth built by living things: tiny coral animals.

caption:
The Great Barrier Reef can be seen from space. 🪸🛰️

It's the largest structure built by living things.

hook: Wombats poop *cubes.*
hookVo: Wombats poop cubes.

scenes.sub: The only animal known to do it.
scenes.vo: Wombats are the only animals known to make cube-shaped poop, up to a hundred cubes a night.
Their intestines have stiff and stretchy sections that mould it into cubes, so it doesn't roll off the rocks where they leave it.

caption:
Wombats poop cubes. 🟫 Yes, really.

Their intestines shape it, and the cubes don't roll away from the spots they mark.

hook: A tree alive today is nearly *5,000 years old.*
hookVo: There's a tree alive today that's nearly five thousand years old.

scenes.vo: A bristlecone pine in California, nicknamed Methuselah, is about four thousand eight hundred years old.
That makes it older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.

caption:
A bristlecone pine called Methuselah is ~4,800 years old. 🌲

It's older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.

hook: Earth has more *trees* than the Milky Way has stars.
hookVo: Earth has more trees than there are stars in the Milky Way.

scenes.vo: There are about three trillion trees on Earth.
Our galaxy has somewhere between one hundred and four hundred billion stars.

caption: Earth has ~3 trillion trees, more than the 100–400 billion stars in the Milky Way. 🌳✨

hook: Some bamboo can grow almost *1 metre* in a day.
hookVo: Some bamboo can grow almost one metre in a single day.

scenes.vo: Some species can grow up to ninety-one centimetres in a single day.

scenes.sub: You could almost watch it grow.
scenes.vo: That's nearly four centimetres an hour. You could almost watch it grow.

caption: Some bamboo can grow up to 91 cm in one day. 🎋

hook: Honey never *spoils.*
hookVo: Honey never spoils.

scenes.vo: Archaeologists have found honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that was around three thousand years old, and still edible.

scenes.ital: Too little water, too much acid.
scenes.vo: Honey has so little water and so much acid that bacteria simply can't survive in it.

caption:
Honey never spoils. 🍯

Archaeologists have found ~3,000-year-old honey in Egyptian tombs that was still edible.

hook: Bananas are *berries.* Strawberries aren't.
hookVo: Bananas are berries. Strawberries aren't.

scenes.big: A berry grows from *one flower* with one ovary.
scenes.vo: In botany, a berry grows from a single flower with one ovary, and bananas fit perfectly.

scenes.ital: Their seeds are on the outside.
scenes.vo: Strawberries don't. Their seeds are on the outside, so they're not true berries at all.

caption: Bananas are berries, but strawberries aren't. 🍌🍓

hook: Lightning is about *5 times* hotter than the Sun's surface.
hookVo: Lightning is about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.

scenes.sub: Hot enough to melt sand into glass.
scenes.vo: A lightning bolt can heat the air to around thirty thousand degrees Celsius.
The surface of the Sun is only about five thousand five hundred degrees.

caption: A lightning bolt can be ~5x hotter than the surface of the Sun. ⚡☀️

hook: Mount Everest is still *growing.*
hookVo: Mount Everest is still growing.

scenes.vo: Everest grows by roughly four millimetres every year.
That's because India is still pushing into Asia, slowly lifting the Himalayas.

caption:
Mount Everest grows ~4 mm every year. 🏔️

India's tectonic plate is still pushing into Asia.

hook: The largest desert on Earth is *Antarctica.*
hookVo: The largest desert on Earth is Antarctica.

scenes.big: A desert is about *rain*, not heat.
scenes.vo: A desert is defined by how little rain or snow it gets, not by heat. And Antarctica barely gets any.
At about fourteen million square kilometres, it's bigger than the Sahara.

caption:
The largest desert on Earth is Antarctica. 🧊

Deserts are defined by low precipitation, not heat.

hook: The Sahara used to be *green.*
hookVo: The Sahara desert used to be green.

scenes.vo: Between about eleven and six thousand years ago, the Sahara had lakes, grasslands and even hippos.

scenes.ital: Earth's slow wobble shifted the monsoons.
scenes.vo: Slow changes in Earth's orbit shifted the monsoon rains, and the desert returned.

caption: The Sahara was green ~6,000–11,000 years ago, with lakes, grassland and hippos. 🌿🐪

hook: Your heart beats about *100,000* times a day.
hookVo: Your heart beats about a hundred thousand times every day.

scenes.vo: At about seventy beats a minute, that's roughly a hundred thousand beats a day.
Over a lifetime, that adds up to around three billion beats, without ever stopping.

caption: Your heart beats ~100,000 times a day, about 3 billion times in a lifetime. ❤️

hook: Babies have nearly *100 more* bones than adults.
hookVo: Babies are born with nearly a hundred more bones than adults.

scenes.vo: A newborn has around three hundred bones.

scenes.sub: Many fuse together as we grow.
scenes.vo: As we grow, many of them fuse together, leaving two hundred and six.

caption:
Babies have ~300 bones; adults have 206. 🦴

Many fuse together as we grow.

hook: Your brain uses about *20%* of your energy.
hookVo: Your brain uses about twenty percent of your body's energy.

scenes.vo: Your brain burns about a fifth of your energy, even while you're asleep.
Yet it's only about two percent of your body weight.

caption: Your brain is ~2% of your body weight but uses ~20% of your energy. 🧠⚡

hook: Your stomach gets a new lining every *few days.*
hookVo: Your stomach replaces its lining every few days.

scenes.ital: The lining is always under attack.
scenes.vo: Your stomach is full of strong acid, so its lining is constantly under attack.
To survive, it replaces its surface cells every three to five days.

caption: Your stomach replaces its surface lining every 3–5 days. 🔁

hook: The DNA in one cell is about *2 metres* long.
hookVo: The DNA in just one of your cells is about two metres long.

scenes.vo: Uncoiled, the DNA in a single cell would stretch about two metres.

scenes.big: All of it could reach the *Sun* and back.
scenes.vo: And all the DNA in your body could stretch to the Sun and back many times over.

caption:
The DNA in one of your cells is ~2 metres long. 🧬

All of yours could reach the Sun and back many times.

hook: You're made of about *37 trillion* cells.
hookVo: You're made of about thirty-seven trillion cells.

scenes.vo: Scientists estimate the human body has about thirty-seven trillion cells.
And millions of them are replaced every single second.

caption: You're made of ~37 trillion cells, and millions are replaced every second. 🔬

hook: Your body actually *glows.*
hookVo: Your body actually glows in the dark.

scenes.ital: About 1,000 times too weak to see.
scenes.vo: Scientists in Japan found the human body gives off a faint light, about a thousand times too weak for our eyes.
It's brightest in the late afternoon, and strongest around the face.

caption: Your body gives off a faint visible glow, about 1,000x too weak for your eyes to see. ✨🧍

hook: You're slightly *taller* in the morning.
hookVo: You're slightly taller in the morning.

scenes.vo: Most people are about a centimetre taller right after they wake up.

scenes.ital: The discs recover while you sleep.
scenes.vo: During the day gravity squeezes the discs in your spine, and they recover while you sleep.

caption:
You're about 1 cm taller in the morning. 📏

Gravity compresses your spinal discs during the day.

hook: Your eyes can tell apart about *1 million* colours.
hookVo: Your eyes can tell apart about a million different colours.

scenes.vo: The human eye can distinguish around a million different colours.
And it does that with only three types of colour-sensing cells.

caption: Your eyes can tell apart ~1 million colours using just 3 types of cone cells. 👁️🌈

hook: Cleopatra lived closer to the *Moon landing* than to the Great Pyramid.
hookVo: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.

scenes.vo: The Great Pyramid was already about two and a half thousand years old when Cleopatra was born.
The Moon landing came only about two thousand years after her.

caption: Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid. 🏺🚀

hook: Oxford University is older than the *Aztec Empire.*
hookVo: Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire.

scenes.vo: Teaching at Oxford began around ten ninety-six.
The Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, wasn't founded until thirteen twenty-five.

caption: Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire. 🏛️

hook: The Great Pyramid was the tallest building for *3,800 years.*
hookVo: The Great Pyramid was the tallest building in the world for about three thousand eight hundred years.

scenes.vo: Built around two thousand five hundred and sixty BC, it stayed the tallest for about three thousand eight hundred years.
It was finally beaten in thirteen eleven, by Lincoln Cathedral in England.

caption: The Great Pyramid was the world's tallest building for ~3,800 years. 🔺

hook: Mammoths were still alive when the *pyramids* were built.
hookVo: Woolly mammoths were still alive when the Great Pyramid was built.

scenes.big: The last mammoths lived on *Wrangel Island.*
scenes.vo: The last woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island until about four thousand years ago.
The Great Pyramid was built about four thousand five hundred years ago.

caption: Woolly mammoths were still alive when the Great Pyramid was built. 🦣🔺

hook: The shortest war in history lasted under *an hour.*
hookVo: The shortest war in history lasted less than an hour.

scenes.vo: In eighteen ninety-six, Britain and Zanzibar fought a war that lasted about thirty-eight minutes.

scenes.big: Over before most people *knew* it started.
scenes.vo: It was over before most people even knew it had started.

caption: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 lasted about 38 minutes. ⏱️

hook: Nintendo was founded in *1889.*
hookVo: Nintendo was founded in eighteen eighty-nine.

scenes.vo: Nintendo started in Kyoto, Japan, in eighteen eighty-nine.

scenes.ital: Video games came almost 90 years later.
scenes.vo: It began by making playing cards. Video games came almost ninety years later.

caption: Nintendo was founded in 1889, as a playing card company. 🎴

hook: The fax machine was invented before the *telephone.*
hookVo: The fax machine was invented before the telephone.

scenes.vo: Scottish inventor Alexander Bain patented an early fax machine in eighteen forty-three.
The telephone was patented thirty-three years later, in eighteen seventy-six.

caption: The fax machine (1843) was invented before the telephone (1876). 📠☎️

hook: You can't see the Great Wall of China from *space.*
hookVo: You can't actually see the Great Wall of China from space with your eyes.

scenes.vo: The wall is incredibly long, but only a few metres wide.
Astronauts say it's basically impossible to spot with the naked eye from orbit.

caption: You can't see the Great Wall of China from space with the naked eye. 🧱🛰️

hook: The first computer bug was a real *moth.*
hookVo: The first computer bug was an actual moth.

scenes.vo: In nineteen forty-seven, engineers found a moth stuck inside the Harvard Mark Two computer.

scenes.big: But the word *bug* was much older.
scenes.vo: But the joke worked because engineers already called glitches bugs. Edison used the word in the eighteen seventies.

caption: The first 'actual case of bug being found' was a moth in 1947, but engineers were already saying 'bug' for decades. 🦋💻

hook: Every good shuffle likely creates an order that's *never existed.*
hookVo: Every time you shuffle a deck properly, you probably create an order that has never existed before.

scenes.vo: A deck has just fifty-two cards.
But they can be arranged in about eight followed by sixty-seven zeros different ways. More than the atoms on Earth.

caption:
A well-shuffled deck is almost certainly in an order that has never existed before. 🃏

52! ≈ 8 × 10^67.

hook: There are more possible chess games than *atoms* in the universe.
hookVo: There are more possible chess games than atoms in the observable universe.

scenes.vo: Mathematician Claude Shannon estimated around ten to the power of a hundred and twenty possible games.
The whole observable universe has only about ten to the power of eighty atoms.

caption: There are more possible chess games (~10^120) than atoms in the observable universe (~10^80). ♟️🌌

hook: In a room of just *23 people*, two probably share a birthday.
hookVo: In a room of just twenty-three people, it's more likely than not that two share a birthday.

scenes.vo: With just twenty-three people in a room...
...the chance two share a birthday is just over fifty percent. With seventy people, it's over ninety-nine point nine.

caption: In a room of 23 people, there's a >50% chance two share a birthday. 🎂🎉

hook: Fold paper *42 times* and it would reach the Moon.
hookVo: In theory, if you folded a sheet of paper forty-two times, it would reach the Moon.

scenes.vo: Each fold doubles its thickness.
After forty-two folds, it would be about four hundred and forty thousand kilometres thick. Past the Moon.

caption: In theory, folding a paper 42 times would make it thick enough to reach the Moon. 📄🌕

hook: Zero wasn't always a *number.*
hookVo: Zero wasn't always treated as a number.

scenes.vo: In six twenty-eight AD, the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta wrote the first known rules for using zero as a number.
Without zero, there'd be no computers. Everything digital runs on zeros and ones.

caption: Zero wasn't always a number. In 628 AD, Brahmagupta wrote the first known rules for it. 0️⃣

hook: The first gigabyte hard drive weighed about *250 kg.*
hookVo: The first gigabyte hard drive weighed about two hundred and fifty kilograms.

scenes.vo: In nineteen eighty, IBM's first gigabyte-class hard drive weighed about two hundred and fifty kilograms.

scenes.sub: Today a tiny card holds far more.
scenes.vo: And it cost around forty thousand dollars.

caption: The first gigabyte hard drive (IBM 3380, 1980) weighed ~250 kg and cost ~$40,000. 💾

hook: Your phone has *millions of times* more memory than Apollo 11's computer.
hookVo: Your phone has millions of times more memory than the computer that took Apollo eleven to the Moon.

scenes.vo: The Apollo guidance computer had only about four kilobytes of working memory.

scenes.big: Your phone has *millions* of times more.
scenes.ital: And Apollo still landed on the Moon.
scenes.vo: A modern phone has millions of times more. And that tiny computer still landed humans on the Moon.

caption: Apollo 11's guidance computer had about 4 KB of memory. Your phone has millions of times more. 🚀📱

hook: The first website ever made is still *online.*
hookVo: The very first website ever made is still online.

scenes.vo: Tim Berners-Lee published it at CERN in nineteen ninety-one.

scenes.ital: You can still visit it today.
scenes.vo: And you can still visit it today, at info dot cern dot ch.

caption: The first website ever made (1991) is still online at info.cern.ch. 🌐

hook: Email is older than the *World Wide Web.*
hookVo: Email is older than the World Wide Web.

scenes.vo: Ray Tomlinson sent the first network email in nineteen seventy-one, and picked the at sign.
The World Wide Web only went public twenty years later, in nineteen ninety-one.

caption: Email (1971) is about 20 years older than the World Wide Web (1991). 📧

hook: Wi-Fi doesn't actually stand for *anything.*
hookVo: Wi-Fi doesn't actually stand for anything.

scenes.vo: It's not short for wireless fidelity. That's a myth.

scenes.ital: Picked by a branding company in 1999.
scenes.vo: It was simply a catchy name picked by a branding company in nineteen ninety-nine.

caption: Wi-Fi doesn't stand for 'Wireless Fidelity', or anything at all. 📶
